units.title: The Earth-Sun Relation
units.intro:
Earth is a planet in the solar system, slightly flattened ball. **Rotation** (spin on its axis, ~24 h) → day and night, apparent daily path of the Sun, Coriolis deflection of winds (preview). Axis tilt ~23½°.

**Revolution** (orbit ~365¼ days) + tilt → seasons: when the northern hemisphere leans toward the Sun it is northern summer (June solstice, Tropic of Cancer 23½°N gets overhead sun). December opposite. Equinoxes: equal day and night, sun over equator.

cards.title: 2.1 Introducing the Universe
body: The universe consists of many types of planets, moons, countless stars, comets, meteors, meteorites, and asteroids.
The universe is also comprised of gasses, dust particles, and other materials of nonastronomical bodies.
The so-called explosion ejected a large quantity of materials in all directions, which may still be expanding.
The universe’s constituent elements could also be categorized into infinite galaxies like the, Milky - Way, and other star systems.
The **Milky Way galaxy** is a large rotating body of stars, dust, gasses and other materials held together by gravity.

lessons.title: Rotation of the Earth and its Effects

cards.title: 2.2 Rotation of the Earth and its Effects
body: The earth rotates on its own axis within the solar system.
The earth is also the only known planet that has humans life.
Earth is constantly rotating on its own axis.
In other words, the sun’s radiation is not uniformly distributed over the surface of the earth.
As already stated, the movement of the earth on its own axis from west to east is called **rotation**.

cards.title: Step by step: Rotation of the Earth and its effects
body: **Step 1:** Rotation is the spinning of the Earth on its own axis, from west to east (anticlockwise seen from above the North Pole).
**Step 2:** One complete rotation takes about 24 hours (23 h 56 min against the stars), which gives one day.
**Step 3:** Effect 1 – day and night: the half facing the Sun has day, the other half night; the circle of illumination separates them.
**Step 4:** Effect 2 – time differences: 360° ÷ 24 h = 15° of longitude per hour, so places east of you are ahead in time.
**Step 5:** Effect 3 – deflection of winds and ocean currents (Coriolis effect): to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern.
**Step 6:** Effect 4 – the slight flattening of the poles and bulging at the equator, and the daily rise and fall of tides.

**Example:** Asmara is at about 39°E and Greenwich at 0°. Difference = 39° ÷ 15° per hour ≈ 2.6 h, so local solar time in Asmara is about 2 h 36 min ahead of Greenwich (official Eritrean time is GMT+3).

cards.title: Mnemonic — D-T-D-F
body: Day and night, Time difference, Deflection, Flattening: the four effects of rotation.

cards.title: Exam tip
body: Do not mix rotation with revolution. Rotation (24 h, on the axis) → day/night and time. Revolution (365¼ days, around the Sun) → seasons and leap years.

**Step 1: Identify geometric effects of Earth's rotation.**
Rotation produces centrifugal force, which flattens the polar regions slightly.

**Step 2: Check the polar flatness value.**
The Earth exhibits approximately **0.3%** flatness over its polar regions.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct percentage is **0.3%**.

cards.why: The Earth is estimated to be about $$ 4.6 $$ billion years old, based on radiometric dating of meteorites and Earth rocks.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: Because of the Earth's rotation, the local time of a place 30° east of Greenwich is:
cards.why:
**Step 1:** The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours, i.e. 15° per hour.

**Step 2:** 30° ÷ 15° per hour = 2 hours.

**Step 3:** Places to the east see the Sun earlier, so they are ahead.

**Tip:** East – gain time (add); west – lose time (subtract).

lessons.title: Revolution of the Earth and its Effects

cards.title: 2.3 Revolution of the Earth and its Effects
body: The plane in which the earth‘s orbit is known as the **plane of ecliptic**.
Around July 44 or 5, for example, the earth reaches at the point in its orbit, which is the farthest from the sun.
Centripetal force, which is the sun’s gravitational force, and centrifugal force which is the earth’s gravitational force, keep the earth moving in a steady direction around the sun.
Solstice: The solstice is the time of the year when the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn experience the overhead sun.
Between March 21 and September 23, which is called the **summer solstice**, the sun is in the northern hemisphere for six months.

cards.title: 3D-style globe (offline)
body: Tilted stick = axis. Rotate. Night is the face away from the “sun” side.

cards.title: SPIN / SWING
body: Rotation = spin = day. Revolution = yearly swing = seasons (only because of tilt). No tilt = no seasons.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the speed of Earth's rotation at the North and South Poles?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze how rotational speed varies with latitude.**
Rotational speed is proportional to the circumference of latitude. Circumference decreases poleward.

**Step 2: Evaluate at the poles.**
At the geographic poles, the latitude circle shrinks to a single point. Its circumference is zero.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Thus, the speed of rotation at the poles is **0 km/h**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The imaginary line of the Earth's axis is inclined to its orbital plane (plane of ecliptic) at an angle of:
cards.why:
**Step 1: Differentiate tilt angles.**
- Tilt from the perpendicular: $$23.5^{\circ}$$
- Tilt from the orbital plane (ecliptic): $$90^{\circ} - 23.5^{\circ} = 66.5^{\circ}$$

**Step 2: Recall the key facts.**
The earth's axis is inclined to the plane of its orbit at an angle of 66.5 degrees (23.5° from the vertical).

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct angle relative to the orbital plane is **66.5 degrees**.

**Step 3: Final Result**
Therefore, the correct angle relative to the orbital plane is **66.5 degrees**.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: The period of time, when the earth is at the farthest distance from the sun is called __________.
cards.why: **Aphelion** is the point in Earth's orbit where it is at its **farthest** distance from the sun (occurring around July 4). **Perihelion** is when it is **closest** (around January 3).

glossary.meaning: A huge system of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.
The time (about 21 June and 22 December) when the overhead sun is over one of the tropics, giving the longest or shortest day.
A force directed towards the centre that keeps a body moving in a curved path; for the planets it is the sun's gravity.
The spiral galaxy that contains our solar system.
The time (about 21 March and 23 September) when the overhead sun is over the equator and day and night are equal everywhere.

tips.text: The spinning of the earth on its own axis from west to east is called rotation.
The earth takes about 24 hours to complete a rotation.
The axial plane of the earth is inclined to the plane of the earth’s orbit at an angle of 66 ½0.
The different kinds of weather that occur over land and bodies of water are the results of the earth’s rotation on its own axis.
The length of day andnight and the apparent movement of the sun are also caused by the earth’s rotation and the angle of its orbital plane as well.
The movement of the earth around the sun is called a revolution.
The earth takes one year or 365 ¼ days to complete one orbit around the sun.
The extra hours are added to make one full day every four years or a leap year.
Due to the elliptical shape of the earth’s orbit the sun appears closer (perihelion) and further (aphelion) from the earth at different seasons of the year.
The revolution of the earth causes the variation of the length of days and nights and, seasons of the year.

questions.answer: About 24 hours.
why: The Earth turns once on its axis in about 24 hours (more exactly 23 h 56 min relative to the stars).

similar.q: The local time difference between 105°E and 180°E is:  A) 5 hours  B) 12 hours  C) 7 hours  D) 24 hours  E) 6 hours
similar.a: A. 5 hours — 75° ÷ 15° = 5 hours. Answer: A.

questions.answer: Day and night.
why: As the Earth rotates, the side facing the Sun has day and the side facing away has night; each place passes through both every 24 hours.
questions.label: 2. Rotation causes?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Days and nights are the result of the  A) rotation of the earth.  B) revolution of the earth.  C) tilting of the Earth's axis.  D) distance between the Sun and Earth.  E) None of the above.
similar.a: A. rotation of the earth. — Revolution (with the tilted axis) causes the seasons and the changing length of day and night, not day and night themselves. Answer: A.

questions.answer: About 365¼ days — leap year extra day.
why: The Earth takes about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun; the extra ¼ day is collected every four years as 29 February.
questions.label: 3. Revolution period?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Days and nights are the result of the  A) rotation of the earth.  B) revolution of the earth.  C) elliptical shape of the earth's orbit.  D) difference in pressure.  E) difference in temperature.
similar.a: A. rotation of the earth. — Revolution around the sun (with the tilted axis) causes the seasons. Answer: A.

questions.answer: About 23½°.
why: The Earth's axis is tilted about 23½° from the perpendicular to the plane of its orbit (66½° to the plane itself).
questions.label: 4. Tilt of the axis?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The movement of the earth on its axis which takes 24 hours is called:  A) annual motion of the earth  B) monthly motion of the earth  C) daily motion of the earth  D) apparent movement of the sun  E) apparent movement of the earth
similar.a: C. daily motion of the earth — Answer: C.

questions.answer: Tilt + revolution change which hemisphere leans toward the Sun.
why: Because the axis stays tilted in the same direction as the Earth orbits, each hemisphere leans towards the Sun for part of the year (summer: higher Sun, longer days) and away from it for the other part (winter).
questions.label: 5. Why seasons?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The variation of seasons in the latitudinal zones of the earth is identified by:  A) the shifting positions of the overhead earth between the hemispheres  B) the shifting positions of the overhead moon between the hemispheres  C) the shifting positions of the overhead sun between the hemispheres  D) centripetal and centrifugal forces keeping and pulling the earth and the sun  E) gradational and tectonic forces of the earth
similar.a: C. the shifting positions of the overhead sun between the hemispheres — Answer: C.

questions.answer: Tropic of Cancer 23½°N.
why: On about 21 June the Northern Hemisphere leans most towards the Sun, and the noon Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, 23½°N.
questions.label: 6. June solstice overhead sun?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: Equinox is the time when the sun is directly over the  A) Equator.  B) Tropic of Cancer.  C) Tropic of Capricorn.  D) North Pole.  E) South Pole.
similar.a: A. Equator. — When the sun is overhead at a tropic it is a solstice (Cancer about 21 June, Capricorn about 22 December). The sun is never overhead at the poles. Answer: A.

questions.answer: Tropic of Capricorn 23½°S.
why: On about 22 December the Southern Hemisphere leans most towards the Sun, and the noon Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, 23½°S.
questions.label: 7. December solstice?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.a: B. December 21. — Answer: B.

questions.answer: Equator. Day ≈ night everywhere.
why: At the equinoxes (about 21 March and 23 September) neither hemisphere leans towards the Sun; the noon Sun is overhead at the equator and day and night are about 12 hours everywhere.
questions.label: 8. Equinox overhead sun?
questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: The rays of the sun are vertical over the equator on  A) June 21 and December 21.  B) March 21 and September 23.  C) June 21 and September 20.  D) January 21 and June 21.  E) None of the above.
similar.a: B. March 21 and September 23. — June 21 and December 21 are the solstices, when the sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. Answer: B.

questions.answer: 24 h light in local summer; 24 h dark in local winter.
why: At the Arctic Circle (66½°N) the Sun does not set on the June solstice (24 hours of daylight) and does not rise on the December solstice (24 hours of darkness).

similar.a: Oblate spheroid (slightly flattened at poles).

questions.answer: Oblate spheroid (slightly flattened at poles).
why: The Earth bulges slightly at the equator and is flattened at the poles because of its rotation, so it is an oblate spheroid (geoid), not a perfect sphere.

similar.q: Identify the wrong idea describing lines of latitude and longitude (meridians):  A) Latitudes are drawn in an east–west direction.  B) Meridians have the same length and narrow towards the top (poles).  C) The equator is 0° and a great circle.  D) The prime meridian is 0° and all meridians are (halves of) great circles.  E) Meridians measure places north–south of the equator.
similar.a: E. Meridians measure places north–south of the equator. — A–D are acceptable descriptions (meridians all meet at the poles and each forms half of a great circle). Answer: E.

why: The poles are the furthest points from the equator, a quarter of a circle away: 90°N and 90°S.

similar.q: Winds that blow from the slowly rotating poles towards the fast-rotating equator are deflected towards the:  A) south-east  B) north-west  C) west  D) east  E) south
similar.a: C. west — The ground under the wind moves eastward faster near the equator, so the wind lags behind, i.e. towards the west. Answer: C (hence the polar EASTERLIES and trade winds blow from the east).

questions.answer: 0° — Greenwich.
why: Longitude is measured east and west from the Prime Meridian (0°), which passes through Greenwich, London.

questions.tip: Say or write your answer first, then open the model answer and compare the key words.

similar.q: An imaginary circle which is equidistant between north pole and south pole is called the  A) Equator.  B) Tropic of Cancer.  C) Tropic of Capricorn.  D) Prime Meridian.  E) International Date Line.
similar.a: A. Equator. — The tropics lie at 23½° N and S, so they are not equidistant from both poles. The Prime Meridian and the Date Line are half-circles joining the poles. Answer: A.

questions.q: Why the Sun “rises in the east”?
questions.answer: Earth rotates west → east.
why: The Earth rotates from west to east, so places on the Earth turn towards the Sun first in the east; the Sun appears to rise in the east and set in the west.

similar.q: Winds that blow from the fast rotating part of the Earth (the equator) to the slow rotating part (pole), deflect towards  A) north.  B) south.  C) east.  D) west.  E) southwest.
similar.a: C. east. — Winds blowing towards the equator lag behind and are deflected west (e.g. NE and SE trade winds). Answer: C.

questions.answer: The Sun. Earth is one planet.
why: The Sun is at the centre of the solar system; the eight planets, including the Earth, orbit it.

questions.answer: No real seasons — same sun angle all year at each latitude.
why: Without tilt the noon Sun would always be overhead at the equator and every place would have the same Sun angle and day length all year, so there would be no seasons.

similar.q: Among the planets in the solar system, the nearest to the sun is  A) Mercury.  B) Venus.  C) Earth.  D) Mars.  E) Jupiter.
similar.a: A. Mercury. — Mercury is the first, nearest the sun. Answer: A.

questions.q: Apparent path of the Sun is caused by?
questions.answer: Earth’s rotation, not the Sun racing around us.
why: The Sun seems to move across the sky from east to west because the Earth rotates from west to east; the Sun is not circling the Earth.

similar.q: Of the planets in the solar system, the nearest to the sun is  A) Mercury.  B) Venus.  C) Earth.  D) Mars.  E) Jupiter.
similar.a: A. Mercury. — Order from the sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune. Answer: A.

questions.q: Overhead sun never happens at 40°N because?
questions.answer: Tropics only — 23½°N to 23½°S.
why: The overhead Sun moves only between 23½°N and 23½°S during the year; 40°N is outside the tropics, so the noon Sun is never directly overhead there.

questions.q: Which motion you do not feel?
questions.answer: Both — we move with the Earth.
why: We, the air and everything around us move with the Earth at a steady speed, so we do not feel either rotation or revolution.

similar.q: The planet in the solar system with a relatively bigger size and lower density is  A) Mercury.  B) Venus.  C) Earth.  D) Mars.  E) Uranus.
similar.a: E. Uranus. — Only Uranus is an outer planet. Answer: E.

questions.q: Seasons are not “closer to the Sun” as the main cause.
questions.answer: Orbit is only slightly oval; tilt dominates seasons.
why: The Earth's orbit is almost circular; in fact the Earth is closest to the Sun in January (northern winter). Seasons are caused by the tilt, which changes the Sun's angle and day length.

similar.q: The distance between the earth and the sun varies during different seasons of the year due to the  A) circular nature of the earth' orbit.  B) elliptical nature of the earth's orbit.  C) gravitational force of the moon.  D) gravitational force of the sun.  E) None of the above.
similar.a: B. elliptical nature of the earth's orbit. — A circular orbit would keep the distance constant. Answer: B.

questions.answer: Latitude and season set the energy budget.
why: Latitude and season control the angle of the Sun and the length of day, which set how much solar energy a place receives — the basis of its climate (Unit 3).
